{
  "reframes": [
    {
      "bottleneck": "The compute axis scales molecule count (8 to 120) under one fixed force field, but the hypothesized error floor is systematic and chemistry-dependent. More molecules with the same force field only measure that floor more precisely; a single global bias correction cannot remove chemistry-dependent bias, so most of the $940 buys better statistics on the same error rather than a smaller error.",
      "assumption": "The force field and its errors are held fixed; only the number of sampled molecules is allowed to grow, and correction is a single global bias term.",
      "reframe": "Redirect compute from more molecules to a chemistry-conditioned correction: regress MD-to-measurement residuals on cheap per-molecule descriptors (carbon number, ester-group count, MD-predicted value) trained on a modest set and validated held-out. Compute then buys a transferable correction applicable to all 835 molecules, not repeated samples of the same bias.",
      "question": "Does a descriptor-based correction trained on 24 molecules' MD-and-measurement pairs reduce held-out viscosity mean absolute percent error below 15% on 8 molecules not used in fitting, at 40 °C?",
      "measure": "Fit a ridge or Gaussian-process regression of signed MD-vs-measurement residuals against descriptors using the published 8 plus 16 new molecules from the already-budgeted 24-molecule stage; score absolute percent error on 8 held-out molecules. The training runs are already paid for; incremental cost is 8 held-out molecules at ~30 ns each, roughly $60–$100, plus negligible analysis time.",
      "compute_after": "Each additional dollar buys training molecules that shrink correction error across the whole 835-molecule set, so more compute changes the ranking answer instead of re-measuring a fixed floor.",
      "exact": "Held-out mean absolute percent error on viscosity, and Spearman rank correlation between corrected MD viscosity and measured viscosity, over 8 molecules excluded from fitting, at 40 °C.",
      "expected": "If the floor is genuinely chemistry-dependent, residuals are structured and held-out error falls to roughly 12–18% at N=24 with rank correlation above 0.85.",
      "fails_if": "Held-out error stays at or above 25% with the correction trained on 24 molecules, meaning residuals carry no chemistry-predictable structure and the floor is effectively random.",
      "closest_prior": "Ogbomo 2026 reports raw LOPLS-AA Green–Kubo errors on 8 molecules with no correction model [s_ogbomo_md]; the planned work scales the same uncorrected protocol [s_ogbomo_res]."
    },
    {
      "bottleneck": "Cost per molecule is dominated by converging the Green–Kubo stress autocorrelation (six 5-ns replicas, ~30 ns per molecule), because the chosen quantity, direct viscosity, is one of the slowest observables to converge. The pipeline's actual need is rank order over hundreds of candidates, so expensive absolute accuracy on few molecules caps coverage.",
      "assumption": "Viscosity and thermal conductivity must be computed directly and at high absolute accuracy in order to rank candidates.",
      "reframe": "Change the measured quantity to a cheaper related one that converges in about 1 ns, such as the self-diffusion coefficient from the mean-squared displacement, combined through a Stokes–Einstein- or Rosenfeld-style scaling with density and size, calibrated to viscosity on a small anchor set. Compute then buys chemical coverage instead of trajectory length.",
      "question": "Does a 1-ns diffusion-derived proxy rank the 8 published benchmark molecules' measured viscosity with Spearman rank correlation of at least 0.8?",
      "measure": "Run one 1-ns trajectory for each of the 8 published molecules, extract the self-diffusion coefficient from the MSD slope, and compute Spearman correlation between the proxy ranking and the measured viscosity ranking. Roughly 8 ns total, on the order of $10–$20, fittable inside the existing check-first stage.",
      "compute_after": "If the proxy preserves order, each GPU-hour covers roughly 20–30 times more molecules, so additional compute directly buys ranking coverage toward the full 835-molecule set rather than longer runs on the same few.",
      "exact": "Spearman rank correlation between proxy-derived ordering (inverse diffusion scaled by density and molecular size) and measured viscosity ordering across the 8 published molecules at 40 °C.",
      "expected": "Correlation around 0.7–0.9 within a homologous series, with the main risk being a systematic offset between hydrocarbons and esters that a two-group calibration would absorb.",
      "fails_if": "Spearman correlation below 0.6 on the 8 molecules, showing the proxy does not preserve order even in-distribution and is not worth calibrating.",
      "closest_prior": "Direct Green–Kubo viscosity on 8 molecules [s_ogbomo_md]; diffusion-based and excess-entropy viscosity scalings are established elsewhere in the liquids literature but unused in this benchmark."
    },
    {
      "bottleneck": "The 8-to-24-to-48-to-120 ladder commits most of the budget before the decisive fact is known: whether the error is between-chemistry systematic (correctable by coverage and calibration) or within-molecule statistical (reducible only by longer runs). The six-replica protocol already produces both variance components, but the plan never decomposes them, so the allocation between more molecules and more nanoseconds is made blind.",
      "assumption": "Deciding whether the floor exists requires the full 120-molecule ladder run with a fixed per-molecule protocol of six 5-ns replicas.",
      "reframe": "Reorder the work: at the 24-molecule stage, decompose per-replica percent errors into between-molecule and within-molecule variance, then let that decomposition choose the allocation. If between-molecule variance dominates, spend on coverage and correction; if within-molecule variance dominates, spend on longer or more replicas per molecule and fewer molecules.",
      "question": "In the 24-molecule run, what fraction of total viscosity error variance is between-molecule (systematic, chemistry-attached) versus within-molecule (replica noise), as measured by a random-effects variance decomposition of per-replica percent errors?",
      "measure": "Fit a random-effects model to the 6 x 24 per-replica viscosity percent errors from the already-budgeted 24-molecule stage and report the intraclass correlation. Incremental cost is essentially $0 on top of the roughly $150–$250 that stage already plans to spend.",
      "compute_after": "Whichever variance component dominates dictates what the remaining roughly $700 buys, so every later dollar is spent on the term that actually limits ranking, and more compute changes the conclusion rather than repeating the same protocol.",
      "exact": "Intraclass correlation, the share of residual variance attributable to molecule identity, in a random-effects fit of per-replica viscosity percent errors at 40 °C over 24 molecules with 6 replicas each.",
      "expected": "The stated hypothesis predicts a high between-molecule share, above about 0.6, which would confirm a correctable chemistry-dependent floor and argue for the correction-model path.",
      "fails_if": "Between-molecule share below about 0.3, meaning error is mostly statistical replica noise; then correction models are dead and the lever is trajectory length per molecule, which the current plan does not vary.",
      "closest_prior": "Ogbomo 2026 reports per-molecule errors for 8 molecules but no replica-level variance decomposition [s_ogbomo_md, s_ogbomo_res]."
    }
  ]
}
